notes: CCRC murder reference; Morgan Smith provocation misdirection led to retrial though fresh psychiatric evidence was refused.

enrichment.short_title: Karimi: murder conviction quashed for Morgan Smith provocation misdirection
key_facts: Karimi, a Kurdish freedom fighter, killed Sirvan Kabadi in December 1996 after learning of his wife's affair with the victim.
At trial he relied on provocation, diminished responsibility based on PTSD, and self-defence; he was convicted of murder and sentenced to life imprisonment.
The Criminal Cases Review Commission referred the case on fresh psychiatric evidence diagnosing enduring personality change after catastrophic experience (EPCC) and on the summing-up.
Dr Mezey and Dr Grounds disagreed with the trial psychiatrist Dr Nayani on diminished responsibility and offered a shifted provocation case based on EPCC.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal on CCRC reference against murder conviction after refusal of leave and extension of time.
enrichment.outcome: Fresh psychiatric evidence was refused; appeal allowed on provocation misdirection, conviction quashed and retrial ordered; section 4(2) reporting restriction imposed.
enrichment.ratio: Where psychiatric evidence relevant to provocation is directed only to diminished responsibility, the jury may be misled and a Morgan Smith misdirection on special characteristics can render a murder conviction unsafe even if fresh expert evidence would not have changed the verdict.
legal_issues: Whether fresh EPCC psychiatric evidence should be admitted under section 23
Whether the summing-up complied with Morgan Smith on provocation
Whether psychiatric evidence was wrongly excluded from the provocation direction
Whether the court should substitute manslaughter or order a retrial
linked_authorities: R v Morgan Smith [2001] 1 AC 146
R v Josephine Smith [2002] EWCA Crim 2671
R v Weller [2004] 1 Cr App R(S) 1
R v Rowland [2003] EWCA Crim 3636

confidence.notes: Grounds for allowing the appeal, refusal of fresh evidence and retrial order are all clearly reasoned.

notes: Third judgment in W v Westminster libel/HRA case; qualified privilege upheld, Article 8 declaration but no damages.

enrichment.short_title: W v Westminster: libel fails on qualified privilege; Article 8 declaration without damages
key_facts: W brought libel and later Human Rights Act claims after Westminster social workers disclosed at a child protection conference that he might be grooming a teenager for prostitution.
The disclosure was made without prior warning to W in the presence of the mother and professionals; the concern arose from earlier unverified file entries.
Eady J had earlier held absolute privilege unavailable; defendants did not plead justification and conceded the words were untrue.
W received an apology and retraction in August 2003 but pursued claims after the council resiled from earlier concessions.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Third Queen's Bench judgment following trial on qualified privilege, malice and a late Human Rights Act Article 8 claim.
enrichment.outcome: Libel claim failed for lack of malice and qualified privilege; declaration that Article 8 was infringed by the disclosure, but no damages as just satisfaction did not require an award.
enrichment.ratio: Qualified privilege may defeat libel even where Article 8 is engaged; misuse of personal information at a child protection conference can breach Article 8 where disclosure was unnecessary, unintentional and made without warning, but damages under section 8 are not mandatory where other remedies suffice.
legal_issues: Whether qualified privilege defeated the libel claim
Whether there was evidence of malice sufficient for a jury
Whether disclosure at the CPC breached Article 8
Whether damages were necessary to afford just satisfaction under section 8(3)
linked_authorities: W v Westminster City Council [2004] EWHC 2866 (QB)
Re S (Sexual Abuse Allegations: Local Authority Response) [2001] 2 FLR 776
Spring v Guardian Assurance plc [1995] 2 AC 296
Chase v News Group Newspapers [2003] EMLR 218

confidence.notes: Final dispositions on libel, Article 8 and remedies are explicit though this is the third instalment of a multi-judgment trial.

notes: Authoritative Court of Appeal ruling that section 24 Limitation Act does not bar winding-up petitions on judgment debts.

enrichment.short_title: Ridgeway Motors v ALTS: no six-year limitation bar to winding-up on judgment debt
key_facts: ALTS, assignee of a 1996 costs judgment exceeding £94,000 with interest, presented a winding-up petition against Ridgeway in 2004.
Ridgeway argued the petition was an action upon a judgment barred after six years under section 24(1) of the Limitation Act 1980.
HHJ Rich QC dismissed the strike-out application but granted a stay pending appeal.
The Revenue sought to intervene as a frequent petitioner but was refused leave, though written submissions were considered.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from refusal to strike out a winding-up petition on limitation grounds.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; presentation of a winding-up petition by a judgment creditor is not subject to the six-year section 24(1) limitation period.
enrichment.ratio: An action upon a judgment in section 24(1) has the special legal meaning of a fresh action to obtain a second judgment, not execution or collective insolvency proceedings; a winding-up petition is sui generis and not statute-barred after six years.
legal_issues: Whether a winding-up petition is an action upon a judgment within section 24(1)
Whether Re a Debtor or Lowsley v Forbes governs insolvency proceedings
Whether the extended definition of action in section 38(1) applies
Whether an ordinary creditor without a judgment is barred from presenting a petition
linked_authorities: Lowsley v Forbes [1999] 1 AC 329
WT Lamb & Sons v Rider [1948] 2 KB 331
Re a Debtor [1997] Ch 310
Re Lines Bros Ltd [1983] Ch 1

confidence.notes: Statutory construction and dismissal are comprehensively reasoned by three members of the court.

notes: Detailed assessment of Greystoke ATE premium after liability-admitted RTA; CPR 44.3B relief granted.

enrichment.short_title: Wooldridge v Hayes: recoverability of ATE premium after admitted-liability RTA
key_facts: The claimant, a patient after severe head injuries in a 1998 road accident, settled for over £600,000 plus costs subject to detailed assessment.
After BTE cover was exhausted, Greystoke ATE insurance was taken out in 2002 at a premium of £7,469 plus IPT to cover opponent's costs under CFA-funded proceedings.
Defendants admitted liability in 1999; the dispute concerned whether the premium, premium-insurance option and automatic increase option were reasonable and recoverable.
The bill failed to comply with CPR Costs Practice Direction requirements on describing cover type until relief was sought.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Detailed assessment before Gray J of disputed ATE insurance premium and insurance premium tax following an approved settlement.
enrichment.outcome: Insurance premium and IPT allowed in full; relief from CPR 44.3B sanction granted; policy terms held not illusory and 10% premium rate reasonable.
enrichment.ratio: An ATE premium may be recoverable where liability was admitted if the risk of failing to beat a Part 36 payment remains real; non-compliance with funding disclosure rules may be relieved where technical and non-prejudicial, and premium reasonableness is judged by burning-cost analysis not website comparators alone.
legal_issues: Whether non-compliance with CPR 44.3B and the Costs Practice Direction barred recovery
Whether Greystoke policy cover was illusory because of conditions 1, 2 and 11
Whether a 10% premium rate was reasonable after liability admission
Whether the premium insurance and automatic increase options were recoverable
linked_authorities: Callery v Gray (No 2) [2001] 1 WLR 2142
Callery v Gray (No 1) [2002] 1 WLR 2000

confidence.notes: Detailed findings on each premium component and sanction relief are explicit.

notes: Care fact-finding appeal; Holman J's paragraph 93 struck out as misstating local authority child protection duties.

enrichment.short_title: North Yorkshire v Swift: failed abuse findings do not bind section 47 protection duties
key_facts: Care proceedings concerned a baby girl whose father had historic but unproven allegations of sexual abuse against two other children.
Holman J at a preliminary fact-finding hearing was not satisfied on the balance of probabilities that either allegation was true.
The judge nevertheless said parties must proceed on the basis the abuse did not happen, while acknowledging very high grounds for suspicion.
The local authority appealed the legal effect of paragraph 93, seeking to maintain child protection register entry and section 47 inquiries.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal with leave limited to statements of law in paragraphs 93-96 after failed threshold findings in care proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed to strike paragraph 93; local authority may continue child protection register entry and section 47(1)(b) inquiries despite unproved section 31 threshold facts.
enrichment.ratio: Failure to prove section 31 threshold facts does not estop a local authority from exercising child protection powers below the care-order threshold; section 47 duties triggered by reasonable cause to suspect significant harm remain distinct from section 31 proof requirements.
legal_issues: Effect of unproved fact-finding on local authority child protection duties
Whether paragraph 93 created res judicata or estoppel
Lawfulness of maintaining the child on the Child Protection Register
Application of section 47(1)(b) after failed threshold findings
linked_authorities: Re H and R (Child Sexual Abuse: Standard of Proof) [1996] 1 FLR 80
Re M and R (Child Abuse: Evidence) [1996] 2 FLR 195
Re S (Sexual Abuse Allegations: Local Authority Response) [2001] 2 FLR 776

confidence.notes: Unanimous Court of Appeal disposal and excision of paragraph 93 are clearly stated.

notes: Judicial review on Pentney FP12 conflict between definitive map and statement; inspector's map presumption quashed.

enrichment.short_title: Norfolk CC v SoS DEFRA: definitive map and statement conflict on Pentney footpath
key_facts: Pentney Footpath No 12 was shown on the definitive map meeting Back Lane at one point but described in the definitive statement as starting at a field gate about 30 metres away.
Norfolk County Council made a 2003 modification order to align the map with the statement; objectors challenged it at a public local inquiry.
The inspector refused confirmation, treating map and statement as irreconcilable and applying a Trevelyan presumption favouring the map.
The Osbornes of Bramborne House had requested the modification after identifying the inconsistency.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of an inspector's decision refusing to confirm a footpath modification order.
enrichment.outcome: Claim upheld; inspector's decision quashed for wrongly applying an evidential presumption in favour of the map over the statement at review stage.
enrichment.ratio: Where definitive map and statement irreconcilably conflict as to a footpath's position, neither document enjoys a review-stage presumption over the other; section 56 makes the map primary for conclusive evidential purposes outside review, but modification decisions require balance-of-probability judgment on all evidence including statement particularity.
legal_issues: Whether the definitive statement prevails over the map as a matter of law
What evidential weight applies at section 53 review when map and statement conflict
Whether the inspector erred by requiring cogent evidence to displace the map
Whether the modification order should have been confirmed in part
linked_authorities: Trevelyan v Secretary of State [2001] 1 WLR 1264
R v Secretary of State ex parte Burrows [1991] 2 QB 354
LE Walwin & Partners Ltd v West Sussex CC [1975] 3 All ER 604
Todd v Secretary of State [2004] 1 WLR 2471

confidence.notes: Detailed four-issue analysis and quashing order are clear though some route-finding facts remain unresolved.

notes: ASBO appeal after vehicle theft; necessity upheld but terms 2-4 struck as disproportionately wide.

enrichment.short_title: McGrath: ASBO partly upheld but ban on all car parks and trespass struck out
key_facts: Jamie McGrath pleaded guilty to theft from a car at St Albans station after DNA linked him to the break-in.
He had an extensive ten-year record of 112 mostly dishonesty offences and received community punishment plus a two-year ASBO.
ASBO terms prohibited all car parks in three counties, all trespass, possession of any tool usable on vehicles, and being drunk in public.
The judge considered McGrath had turned over a new leaf but held an ASBO necessary given his history of station car park offending.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal with leave against sentence limited to the post-conviction ASBO imposed at Luton Crown Court.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed in part; terms 2-4 struck out as draconian, unclear or overlapping with going equipped; terms 1 and 5 upheld for two years.
enrichment.ratio: A post-commencement qualifying offence permits an ASBO where post-1999 antisocial conduct and necessity are shown, with pre-commencement conduct relevant to necessity; ASBO terms must be clear and commensurate with the risk as breach may lead to five years' imprisonment.
legal_issues: Whether pre-commencement conduct could be considered for ASBO necessity
Whether dishonesty offending could support an ASBO
Whether prohibited acts must themselves cause harassment alarm or distress
Whether terms banning all car parks, trespass and tool possession were proportionate
linked_authorities: R v Shane Tony P [2004] EWCA Crim 287

confidence.notes: Statutory framework, partial success and term-by-term analysis are clearly set out.

notes: Major VAT appeal; Telewest restructuring created separate zero-rated magazine supply despite integrated customer package.

enrichment.short_title: Telewest v HMRC: VAT zero-rating restored for Cable Guide magazine supply
key_facts: Telewest supplied cable television and Cable Guide magazine to customers through regional companies until CPP and BSkyB changed VAT composite-supply analysis.
From January 2000 Telewest incorporated Publications Ltd outside the VAT group and used agency arrangements to bill £3.25 magazine charges separately.
Existing customers were notified in Cable Guide; new contracts stated Publications would supply the magazine while regional companies acted as collection agents.
HMRC contended the package remained a single standard-rated supply by Telewest despite the contractual restructuring.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from VAT Tribunal and High Court dismissing Telewest's challenge to standard-rating of magazine element of subscriptions.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; separate contract and VAT supply by Publications to customers established; cross-appeal dismissed; no reference to the Court of Justice.
enrichment.ratio: Domestic contract analysis may support two taxable persons and two VAT supplies where customers acquiesced in partial novation; CPP principal/ancillary supply doctrine does not fuse supplies by different taxable persons, and artificiality arguments cannot override autonomous Community law supply concepts.
legal_issues: Whether existing customers assented to partial novation with Publications
Whether new customer contracts created a separate magazine supply
Whether CPP/BSkyB composite supply principles applied across two suppliers
Whether section 47(2A) VATA treated the regional company as principal supplier of magazines
linked_authorities: Card Protection Plan Ltd v CCE (1999) STC 270
British Sky Broadcasting v CCE (1999) V & DR 283
CCE v Wellington Private Hospital [1997] STC 445
Nell Gwynn House Maintenance Fund Trustees v CCE [1999] STC 79

confidence.notes: Contract and VAT conclusions are detailed though the scheme's fact pattern is complex.

notes: TCC trial on M27 subcontract; JP Mac failed to prove continuing contract with Hanson after mobilisation cap.

enrichment.short_title: JP Mac v Hanson: subcontract transferred to AAL after £20,000 mobilisation work
key_facts: JP Mac supplied operatives and plant on the M27 renewal joint venture between Hanson and Stenoak/AAL.
Hanson contended only initial mobilisation work up to £20,000 was under its subcontract; further work was contracted with AAL, which paid invoices until insolvency.
Mr McCarthy claimed he was told invoicing AAL was quicker and easier; Hanson invoices produced later were found to be manufactured.
Associated Asphalt became insolvent in June 2002 leaving unpaid invoices of £164,816.59 which JP Mac sought from Hanson.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Technology and Construction Court trial on liability for unpaid subcontract sums after joint venture partner insolvency.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; JP Mac proved only the initial Hanson contract to £20,000 and agreed thereafter to contract with AAL/Stenoak under self-billing arrangements.
enrichment.ratio: Where a subcontractor continues work after a capped mobilisation package without objecting to a new party's subcontract documents and self-billing instructions, acquiescence and contemporaneous invoicing to the new paymaster can establish a new contractual relationship despite later fabricated documents.
legal_issues: Whether JP Mac's subcontract remained with Hanson throughout the M27 works
Whether Mr McCarthy agreed to contract with AAL after mobilisation
Effect of self-billing 'THIS IS NOT A TAX INVOICE' endorsements on AAL invoices
Whether adverse inferences should be drawn from absent witnesses and fabricated Hanson invoices

confidence.notes: Findings depend heavily on documentary and credibility analysis but final disposition is clear.

notes: Costs judgment in Richards v Pembrokeshire CC; two-thirds costs after partially successful planning appeal.

enrichment.short_title: Richards v Pembrokeshire: two-thirds costs after successful planning rights appeal
key_facts: Mr and Mrs Richards successfully challenged a Pembrokeshire County Council order affecting their property rights, requiring appeal to the Court of Appeal.
The court initially proposed full costs save for no order on a 9 March 2004 hearing, then invited submissions.
The council argued the appellants raised unsuccessful arguments and changed their case between stages, wasting costs.
Written submissions were exchanged in November and December 2004 after the principal appeal decision.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Supplemental Court of Appeal ruling on costs following substantive success in a planning judicial review appeal.
enrichment.outcome: No order for costs of the 9 March 2004 hearing; otherwise the respondent pays two-thirds of the appellants' costs below and on appeal.
enrichment.ratio: A successful appellant with a justified complaint should normally recover costs, but a significant one-third deduction is appropriate where the winning party changed its case and pursued arguments that wasted court time and opponent's costs without losing entitlement entirely.
legal_issues: Whether the appellants should recover all costs of the appeal and proceedings below
Whether no order should apply to the 9 March 2004 hearing
Effect of case refinements and unsuccessful arguments on costs allocation
Whether exceptional circumstances were needed to deprive a successful party of costs

confidence.notes: Costs order is clear though detailed reasons are summarised rather than fully reported.
